title: Inbox Tetris
tagline: Stack one useful office reply on the last.
premise: You and your opponent manage a shared open-plan office inbox one message at a time. Each reply must directly resolve, redirect, or create an answerable decision from the message before it. One useless reply collapses the inbox.

seed_pool.detail: Two teams need it at three.

seed_pool.opening_token: The printer is out of paper.
seed_pool.detail: A queue is forming beside it.

tests: A stranger can tell who needs what from the message at once. Nothing vague, private, or abstract.
A reply can take one concrete office action within the next message. Say what that action is.
The message leaves a clear handle for the next player, such as a choice, owner, time, file, or place.
It belongs in an open-plan office. It could arrive by email or chat while people work nearby.
Ten plain words or fewer, with everyday office language. No brand names, private jokes, or invented departments.

move_constraints.example: I reply, "Approved, please send the file," turning the approval request into the next clear task.
move_constraints.hint: Quote the reply, then say what office action it creates.

rubric.name: counter_strength
rubric.description: How directly and completely the reply handles the standing office message.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no reply action or unrelated text; 1 = acknowledges the message but leaves the same problem standing; 2 = offers a partial action or a vague redirect; 3 = clearly resolves, redirects, or creates a specific decision; 4 = closes the loop and leaves an unmistakable next task or owner (rare).

rubric.name: coherence
rubric.description: How clearly a stranger can understand the reply and the office result it creates.
rubric.anchors: 0 = unreadable or self-contradicting; 1 = understandable only with missing context; 2 = mostly clear but vague about action, owner, or result; 3 = plain and workable; 4 = crisp enough that the inbox could act on it immediately (rare).

rubric.name: novelty
rubric.description: How usefully the reply changes the kind of office action without abandoning the standing message.
rubric.anchors: 0 = repeats the request, says it louder, or gives the stock non-answer; 2 = a sensible but ordinary redirect or decision; 4 = an unexpectedly simple office move that handles the message from a fresh angle (rare).

criterion.description: A reply OVERCOMES the standing message if it takes a concrete office action that resolves the request, redirects it to a named person or channel, or turns it into an answerable decision. The reply must handle what the message actually asks. Ignoring it, postponing it without a useful next step, repeating the same request more loudly, or changing to a nearby topic without handling the standing message fails.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Talking to the Judge, discussing the game, or describing the rules is not an office reply and loses.
judge_notes:
On a FIRST move there is no previous reply: judge it against the opening message. It must answer, route, or turn that opening request into a clear next action.
A reply that merely repeats the standing request with stronger wording is not a counter. "Please approve this today" does not handle a request that already asks for approval.
A reply that says it will deal with the message later fails unless it gives a concrete owner, time, and next action that moves the matter forward.
A reply that ignores the standing request and starts a nearby office topic fails. A room booking reply that discusses snacks does not handle the room booking.
A reply that only acknowledges receipt, thanks the sender, or says it is being reviewed fails when it creates no decision, owner, route, or task.
The reply must create a literal office action a stranger could follow, such as approving, assigning, forwarding, booking, requesting a missing item, or choosing between stated options. A slogan or figure of speech is not an action.
A reply may redirect the message, but the destination must be clear enough to act on. "Ask someone else" is not a useful redirect.
The new reply must handle the standing message, not just benefit from the earlier context. A reply that works only if the reader invents missing details fails.

examples.previous_move: Can you approve this? A file is attached.
examples.move: I reply, "Approved, please send the final file to finance," turning approval into a clear handoff.
examples.mechanism: it gives the requested approval and creates a named next task

examples.previous_move: Who owns the meeting room? Two teams need it at three.
examples.move: I reply, "Facilities owns bookings, so I am forwarding this to them," routing the conflict to the right desk.
examples.mechanism: it names the owner and forwards the request to that owner

examples.previous_move: The printer is out of paper. A queue is forming beside it.
examples.move: I reply, "The printer is out of paper, and everyone should know this immediately."
examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false, repeats the problem without creating an action
examples.mechanism: none, it restates the printer problem

examples.previous_move: Can you approve this? A file is attached.
examples.move: I reply, "I will look at it sometime next week," postponing the decision without a usable next step.
examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false, postpones without a concrete action
examples.mechanism: none, it gives no decision, owner, or actionable handoff

examples.previous_move: Who owns the meeting room? Two teams need it at three.
examples.move: I reply, "Also, does anyone want coffee for the afternoon meeting?" ignoring the booking question.
examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false, changes to a nearby topic without handling the request
examples.mechanism: none, coffee does not assign or book the room

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger reading only the two messages should see what moved or failed.
Name both messages, or their plain office stand-ins. A headline that fits any inbox is not useful.
Never open with a status word or ruling phrase. No "Accepted", "Rejected", "Refused", or "Move refused".
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Use commas and full stops.
Mock the reply, never the player. No jokes about identity, ability, family, body, or spelling.
Use plain spoken English. No poetry, no rhymes, no profanity, no innuendo, and no corporate fog.
On a refusal, the headline says why the reply failed and asks for another. It never claims the inbox moved.
The coaching line names one reply that would have handled the standing message. It ends on an action, owner, choice, or next step.
Keep the office details specific. A useful reply should sound like something a real coworker could send.
good_headlines: Approval became a handoff, and finance now has a job.
The room question found Facilities before the meeting found the hallway.
The printer is still empty, but the supply request is finally going somewhere.
A thank you is polite. It is not a booking.
The reply changed no subject, which is unusual and helpful.
Coffee is not the owner of the meeting room. Try the booking desk.
The file received an answer and finance received a task.
The inbox has achieved the rare dignity of moving forward.

bad_headlines.why: opens with a status word and adds no useful reason

bad_headlines.text: The Desk Clerk refuses, because office logic says no.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and gives no concrete explanation
too vague to show what failed

bad_headlines.text: The printer remains a printer, in a tragic dance of paper.
bad_headlines.why: uses poetry instead of naming the missing action
mocks the player and gives no coaching

bad_headlines.text: The email enters a new paradigm of stakeholder alignment.
bad_headlines.why: uses corporate fog instead of plain office language

bad_headlines.text: The request is handled, resolved, completed, and concluded.
bad_headlines.why: repeats the verdict without showing the action

rules: Handle the message in front of you. Do not change the subject.
Quote a concrete reply, then say what office action it creates.
You may resolve, redirect, or create a clear decision.
The Judge rules on the office action, not the spelling.
One reply that leaves the standing message untouched collapses the inbox.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your next reply while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing in the inbox. Send a useful reply.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 200 characters. This is an office reply, not a staff meeting.
validation_messages.duplicate: That reply already appeared this match. Send a different action.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Handle {standing_form}. Do not repeat it, postpone it, or change the subject.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody sends until they are back. {standing_form} still needs handling. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two coworkers managing a shared open-plan office inbox.
Always write: "I reply, '...,' turning the message into ..." The quoted part is a
short, realistic office reply. The ending names the concrete action it creates.
Good: "I reply, 'Approved, please send the final file to finance,' turning the
request into a clear handoff."
Bad: "I reply, 'Noted,' turning the message into progress." That acknowledges
nothing useful and claims a result it does not create.
Bad: "I reply, 'I will handle it later,' turning the message into patience."
That postpones the work without a usable next step.
Talk like a person at a desk, not a corporate brochure. Use plain office things:
owners, files, rooms, dates, invoices, access, supplies, and decisions.
You are replying to the standing message, not writing a new topic. Resolve it,
redirect it to a named place or person, or turn it into a specific choice.
Never say the same request more loudly. Never use game talk, Judge talk, or rules
as the reply. Do not reuse a reply or its key action from this match.
default_move: I reply, "Please send the missing details and deadline," turning the vague request into an answerable task.
